reference.source: Manson's Tropical Diseases / Mandell, Douglas and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases
clinicalPearls: Bejel is a chronic non-venereal treponematosis caused by Treponema pallidum subspecies endemicum, occurring in dry, arid regions such as the Sahel, parts of the Middle East and Central Asia
Transmission is non-sexual, by mouth-to-mouth contact or by sharing drinking and eating utensils, mainly among children in dry rural communities
The primary lesion is often unnoticed; disease typically presents in the secondary stage with mucous patches of the mouth and oropharynx and moist condyloma-like lesions in skin folds
Secondary features include angular stomatitis (split papules at the mouth angles), laryngitis and generalised skin lesions, with osteoperiostitis of long bones
Late (tertiary) bejel produces gummatous destruction of skin, nasopharynx and bone, including gangosa, similar to late yaws
Serology and dark-field microscopy are indistinguishable from those of venereal syphilis and the other endemic treponematoses
Treatment of the endemic treponematoses uses benzathine penicillin, with a macrolide alternative for penicillin-allergic patients and mass-treatment campaigns
reference.pathophysiology: Treponema pallidum subspecies endemicum is transmitted through direct mucosal contact or shared utensils in communities with limited hygiene. After entering through the oral mucosa or skin the treponeme multiplies locally and disseminates, producing mucosal and cutaneous secondary lesions and bone involvement over weeks to months. A latent phase may be followed years later by destructive tertiary gummatous lesions of skin, bone and the nasopharynx. As with yaws, the cardiovascular and neurological complications and congenital transmission characteristic of venereal syphilis are not features of bejel.
additionalDifferentials: Oral candidiasis or other causes of mucous patches
Other causes of destructive nasopharyngeal lesions (e.g. leishmaniasis, rhinoscleroma)
additionalInvestigations: Dark-field microscopy of mucosal or skin lesion exudate for spirochaetes
Non-treponemal serology (e.g. RPR/VDRL) for activity and follow-up
PCR of lesion material where available to support subspecies context
Radiographs for osteoperiostitis in symptomatic bones
Assessment of household and community contacts
redFlags: Airway or swallowing compromise from laryngeal or oropharyngeal involvement
Extensive gummatous bone destruction with deformity
Difficulty distinguishing from venereal syphilis in adolescents or adults
reference.prognosis: Early bejel responds well to penicillin with full recovery, but untreated late disease may cause permanent, disfiguring destruction of the oronasopharynx and bone; the endemic treponematoses are targets for elimination programmes.
pitfalls: Misinterpreting positive treponemal serology as venereal syphilis, with inappropriate social and clinical implications
Overlooking the largely unnoticed primary stage and only recognising disease when secondary lesions appear
Failing to treat contacts and address shared-utensil transmission
Confusing bejel with yaws or pinta without geographic and clinical context
Neglecting nutritional and hygiene factors in affected communities
references: Mandell, Douglas and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases
management: Give penicillin, using long-acting intramuscular benzathine penicillin, as first-line curative therapy
Use a macrolide such as azithromycin as an oral alternative in line with endemic-treponematosis programmes, or doxycycline for penicillin-allergic non-pregnant patients
Screen and treat household and community contacts to interrupt transmission
Follow non-treponemal serology (RPR or VDRL) after treatment to confirm response and detect relapse
Provide reconstructive and supportive care for disfiguring late gummatous destruction of the oronasopharynx and bone
Improve hygiene and reduce sharing of eating and drinking utensils, and coordinate with public-health elimination programmes for endemic treponematoses
